strings.old: [Appraise Goods] — Form nine, clause four: perishable household stock is exempt from queue hold. The tin is not perishable, the salt packed with it is, and after four cycles both are still on one manifest line, so the exemption covers the crate.
strings.new: [Appraise Goods] — Form nine, clause four: perishable household stock is exempt from queue hold. The tin is not perishable and the salt packed with it is, and four cycles of manifests have listed the two on one line, so the exemption reaches the crate.

strings.old: The order in the stack is doing work of its own. Appraise it properly and the clause is in there.
strings.new: The forms are stacked in filing order, oldest at the bottom — appraise the stack and the clause comes out of it.

strings.old: Half the jars are from tiers you will never have a permit for. The keeper does not explain how, and you decide not to ask in a city this fond of paperwork.
strings.new: Tier stamps on the jar shoulders. Half of them are numbers your permit does not reach. The keeper watches you read them and goes back to her tally.

strings.old: Bar stock stacked by gauge, each bundle strapped and tagged. The tags carry a tier number, a bench number, and nothing else. No names anywhere on them.
strings.new: Bar stock in strapped bundles, sorted by gauge. Wrist-thick at the bottom of the rack, pencil-thin at the top. The paper tag on each bundle gives a tier number and a bench number.

strings.old: Cooled slag and cracked crucible shards, heaped no higher than a line painted on the flagstones around it. The line has been repainted recently, and brightly.
strings.new: Cooled slag and cracked crucible shards, heaped to just under a line painted on the flagstones around the pile. Fresh paint on the line, the brush marks still crisp at the edges.

strings.old: You put a hand on the rail. Warm from the tier, not from the drop, and cold air comes up the shaft against your wrist.
strings.new: You lean on the bronze rail. Warm brass under your palm; from the shaft, cold air and the clank of the cage somewhere below.

strings.old: A rack of numbered slips beside the second bench: a stock number, a bench number, an hour. No names on any of them. Any pair of hands that can read a gauge can take one down.
strings.new: A rack of numbered slips beside the second bench. A stock number, a bench number and an hour on each one; no name on any of them.

strings.old: A wide iron-strapped door standing open on its wedge. Past it: a working hall, and a heat that has its own weather.
strings.new: A wide iron-strapped door wedged open on the sill, and past it the hall runs hotter and louder than the tier does.

strings.old: You get the pallet onto the loading square and the strapping squared. The attendant looks at it, looks at the bell, and says nothing.
strings.new: You walk the pallet the last hand's width onto the loading square and square the strapping after it. The attendant looks at the load, then writes an hour beside it on the cage slate.

strings.old: Tool racks, empty for the moment, and the bench still ticking as it cools.
strings.new: The bench ticks twice under your hand as it cools, and the racks above it are empty down to the pegs.

strings.old: A bronze grate exhales a slow white breath, steady as a held note. Somewhere below, something enormous is always working.
strings.new: A bronze floor grate breathing white steam in slow pushes. The flags around it carry a beat you can feel through your boots.

strings.old: A Drake in a scarred leather apron, forearms banded with old burn-marks she stopped covering years ago. She works without looking up, and the work doesn't suffer for it.
strings.new: A Drake in a leather apron scarred through in three places, both forearms banded with old burn-marks. Her eyes stay on the colour of the billet; her free hand finds the tongs without going to look for them.

strings.old: A Drake in a brass-buttoned lift coat, one hand resting on the gate lever without gripping it. He watches the counterweights instead of the passengers, and knows where both are.
strings.new: The lift coat is brass-buttoned to the throat, and the Drake wearing it keeps one hand along the gate lever without closing on it. He calls the quarter bell a beat before the cage comes up into the frame.

strings.old: Heat, metal, and a gauge you cannot read. Guessing here costs somebody a week.
strings.new: The gauge on the bench is reading in marks you do not know. Setting the count by guess would spoil the billet and the week of work in it.

strings.old: Colour, count, quench. Two of those you can judge by eye; the count wants a trained one.
strings.new: Colour and quench you can read off the billet yourself. The count between them takes a trained eye — appraise it and the numbers come clear.

strings.old: A civic notice pinned at eye height, examiner's seal at the corner, the text underneath it read so often the ink has gone grey where thumbs land.
strings.new: The examination standard, pinned at eye height. The examiner's seal sits in the corner. Two grey thumbprints in the margin, where everyone holds it to read.

strings.old: Water gone grey with scale, a skin of oil across the top, and a scum line three fingers above the current level.
strings.new: Grey water under a skin of oil, and a scum line ringing the tub three fingers above where the level stands now.

strings.old: Finished pieces racked in a grid, each with a civic tag wired to it and not one price among them.
strings.new: Finished work racked in a grid, wall to wall, each piece with a civic tag wired through it. The tags carry marks and measures; not one of them carries a price.

strings.old: The rig swings past its own marks and settles wrong, again and again. Fixing it belongs to the smith, and she has not asked you to.
strings.new: The rig overshoots its marks and settles wrong, then does it again while you watch. The smith has not asked you to put a hand on it.

strings.old: [Eagle Eyes] — The haze gives up. Nine tiers resolve into stalls, patrol routes, and one dropped coin purse on a ledge two floors down.
strings.new: [Eagle Eyes] — The haze thins: nine tiers of stall rows and patrol routes below the rail. Two floors down, a dropped coin purse sits on a ledge with its drawstring still knotted.

strings.old: No more dropped coins by the railing today.
strings.new: The haze has closed back over the tiers below; come back to the rail after a night's sleep.

strings.old: [Low-Grade Synthesis] — Crude reagents over a low flame, and a draught that mostly does what it should. It will pass.
strings.new: [Low-Grade Synthesis] — Cheap reagents over a low flame, stirred until the colour holds. The draught comes out cloudy and does most of what a draught should.

strings.old: A bulb of dark glass over cold coals, half full of something grey. Not your trade.
strings.new: A bulb of dark glass over cold coals, half full of grey wash. The wash takes one particular heat, and nothing on the retort tells you which.

strings.old: The best bench Xif owns, kept for work you cannot do yet.
strings.new: Xif's own bench, and the burner under the good glass is cold. Lighting it for a true synthesis is work your hands have not learned.

strings.old: The bench Xif keeps for himself: clean glass, a steady blue burner, and room laid out for two reagents to become a third.
strings.new: The bench Xif keeps for himself. Clean glass in a rack, two empty measures set side by side at the front edge. The blue flame under it burns without a flicker.

strings.old: A rank of low carts for hire, each chalked with a tier number and a rate, and a queue board nobody is standing at.
strings.new: Low carts in a rank with their shafts down, each chalked with a tier number and a rate. The queue board beside them is wiped clean, and nobody is standing at it.

strings.old: A stall built to the same civic pattern as every other on this tier — same counter height, same awning pitch, same posted-price placard. Efficient. Impersonal.
strings.new: First of three stalls in a row, and the counter comes to the same height as the next two. A civic inspector's initials are burned into the corner post.

strings.old: Forms, inkwells, and a bell that has clearly been rung far too many times.
strings.new: You put your weight on the ledge where everyone else does. On the other side of it, a clerk turns a form face down and rings the bell for the next in line.
